column1: # AI-rhetoric lint patterns for deck prose.
# Format: id<TAB>severity<TAB>ERE pattern<TAB>message
# Severities: error (the `decks hook lint` write hook denies, `decks lint` and
# `decks check` exit 1, beats.test.ts fails a story card), warn (report only).
# Project terminology rows (id prefix terminology-) go at the bottom; see
# .claude/rules/project-glossary.md.
# Apostrophes/quotes: match straight AND curly via ('|’) style groups, never
# bracket expressions — brackets split multibyte chars if the locale falls
# back to C.
# Sentence-start anchoring: prose lines reach grep as "NR<TAB>ALLOW<TAB>TEXT",
# so ^ anchors the line prefix, not the prose. Use (^|[[:space:]]|"|“) plus a
# required capital letter to approximate sentence start.
# Errors should be near-zero-false-positive (the hook denies writes on them).
# Structural/cadence patterns stay warn: they are sometimes legitimate craft,
# and the goal is guiding judgment, not banning devices humans also use.
# WHAT THIS FILE CANNOT DO (do not re-litigate; re-measure instead):
# These patterns were fitted to a corpus of published data-journalism articles.
# Measured 2026-07-24 on that corpus: 1 hit across 44 shipped articles. The counts drift
# as articles ship — re-run the command rather than trusting this number; the
# finding that survives is the ORDER OF MAGNITUDE, not the digits.
# On the education-data-for-state-agencies article the set produced ZERO hits,
# and that article then needed nine separate user corrections for AI slop.
# Examples that pass clean here: "That finding held at every level below it." /
# "Cleaned once, the same data comes back readable." / "So go find your own
# state's line."
# That is not a coverage bug to patch by adding patterns. Those defects are
# REFERENTIAL and SEMANTIC (a callback with no antecedent, a sentence carrying
# no new fact, a metaphor where a noun belongs). Detecting them requires
# resolving meaning across sentences, which regex cannot do. Every attempt to
# express one as a pattern lands on either "too broad, blocks correct writing"
# or "too narrow, evaded by the next paraphrase" — e.g. a chart-restatement
# rule cannot distinguish slop from the REQUIRED practice of stating a finding
# in prose next to its chart.
# So: this file is a lexical guard (banned words, em-dashes, terminology). It
# is NOT prose review. Empty sentences, chart restatement, and audience
# mismatch are caught by a reviewer's judgment, not here. Never
# report "lint clean" as evidence the prose is good; it measures a domain that
# barely overlaps with prose quality.
# Before adding a pattern, check it fires on the shipped corpus:
#   decks lint          (every registered deck; `bun run lint` in the Decks repo)
# A pattern that never fires is dead weight that manufactures false confidence.
# THE "SAY IT PLAINLY" SET (added 2026-08-31, the ten warns at the bottom).
# The user's single most-repeated correction is a claim arranged across two
# sentences instead of stated in one. Derived by mining 154 session transcripts
# for prose-style complaints that QUOTED the offending sentence, which yielded
# ~46 flagged sentences; patterns were fitted to those, then counted against the
# 49-article shipped corpus. Recall is flagged sentences matched, corpus is raw
# hits across all 49 articles:
#   is-real             recall 2   corpus 36
#   matters-signal      recall 3   corpus 19
#   whole-answer        recall 1   corpus  9
#   cleft-reveal        recall 1   corpus  9
#   negation-assertion  recall 3   corpus  8
#   worth-signal        recall 3   corpus  8
#   hard-to-ignore      recall 1   corpus  7
#   real-question       recall 0   corpus  4
#   metaphor-line       recall 1   corpus  0
#   telling             recall 1   corpus  0
# ALL WARN, DELIBERATELY. They fire on published prose at roughly 2 hits per
# article, because the good and bad uses share the surface form and differ only
# in whether the sentence states a fact or merely characterizes one. Regex cannot
# see that difference. These guide a reviewer; a hit is not itself a defect.
# Rejected as too noisy to be useful, do not re-add without new evidence:
#   ", not (a|an|the|just|merely|simply) "   128 corpus hits
#   "which is (why|the|what|where|how)"       32 corpus hits
#   "genuinely"                               26 corpus hits
# One promotion is on deck: `is-real`. The user calls "X is real" a confirmed
# tell, and all 36 corpus hits inspected were genuine ("The data is real", "The
# cost is real", "The by-major table is real. The sector split is real."). It
# stayed warn only because promoting it would have failed lint on 36 shipped
# articles in that corpus. Scrub your own decks first, then make it an error.
# The judgment-level guidance lives in .claude/rules/deck-writing.md and
# .claude/rules/prose-patterns.md. This file stays a lexical guard, not prose
# review.
em-dash
column4: Em-dash in prose. Use period, comma, colon, or parens.

column1: banned-phrase
column3: [Hh]ere('|’)?s the (thing|kicker)|[Ll]et that sink in|[Rr]ead that again|[Ww]here it gets (interesting|wild|weird)|[Aa]t its core|[Ii]t(('|’)| i)s worth noting|[Mm]ake no mistake|[Tt]he bottom line|[Ff]ull stop
column4: Banned AI-tell phrase. State the fact directly.

column1: not-just-reveal
column4: Not just X, Y escalation. Say what it IS, once.

column1: ai-vocab
column4: AI-marketing vocabulary. Plain words.

column1: inflated-significance
column4: Inflated significance. Say the concrete change, or cut it.

column1: significance-claim
column3: represent(s|ed|ing) a (significant|fundamental|major) shift|part of a broader (movement|shift)
column4: Significance claim. Fine if the article shows it; otherwise say the concrete change.

column1: parallel-reveal
column4: Setup-then-reveal cadence ("X happened. That's why/how/what...").

column1: colon-reveal
column3: : (that('|’)?s|in other words|put simply|translation)|[Ii]n other words,|[Pp]ut (simply|another way)|[Ss]imply put|[Tt]o put (that|it) in(to)? perspective|Translation:
column4: Restatement filler.

column1: folksy-restate
column4: Number restated as a reveal. State the ratio directly instead of stacking it after the raw figure.

column1: powerful
column4: Usually a tell; say what it does.

column1: rhetorical-answer
column4: Rhetorical question answered immediately. State the point as a sentence.

column1: transition-opener
column4: AI transition opener. Cut it; if the point matters, show why.

column1: false-range
column4: False range ("everything from X to Y"). Name the actual examples.

column1: unearned-profundity
column4: Unearned profundity. State what actually happened.

column1: copula-inflation
column4: Inflated copula. "Is" usually works.

column1: participial-tic
column4: Trailing participial importance claim. End the sentence, or replace it with a fact.

column1: literary-ai
column4: Literary-AI decoration. Inform, don't decorate.

column1: negation-assertion
column4: Negation then assertion ("X is not A. It is B."). Say what it IS, once.

column1: matters-signal
column4: Importance claim instead of a fact. Say what changes, not that it matters.

column1: is-real
column4: X is real asserts significance without adding a fact. State the fact.

column1: worth-signal
column4: Announcing that something deserves attention. Name it and let the reader see why.

column1: whole-answer
column4: Characterizing the finding instead of stating it. State the finding.

column1: real-question
column4: Ranking a fact above others instead of stating it.

column1: hard-to-ignore
column4: Importance signal. Give the number that makes it hard to ignore.

column1: metaphor-line
column4: Metaphor standing where a plain noun belongs.

column1: cleft-reveal
column4: Cleft sentence ("What worked was X"). Write "X worked".

column1: telling
column4: Telling claims significance. Say what it tells you.
